newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar says 500 people missing after storm.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar says 500 people missing after storm.

text.p: Madagascar said on Wednesday 500 people were missing and 34 were confirmed dead after a storm hit the northwest of the island at the weekend.
Population Minister Didier Ramaromisa, government spokesman, also said considerable damage was caused by tropical depression Josie which dumped large amounts of rain on the vanilla-growing northwest.
He said floodwaters reached 3.6 metres (12 feet) high when rivers burst their banks because of the rain at the weekend and a total of 500 people were missing and 34 were confirmed dead.
He said 20 people were killed at Antalaha, 11 people were killed at Andapa and three people were killed at Maroantsetra.
Antalaha was cut off because of damaged and flooded roads until Tuesday. State radio said on Tuesday the worst-hit town was Maroantsetra, where residents took to small boats to escape floods.
Josie struck in the northwest of the worlds fourth largest island as work was under way in the southeast to feed and shelter the homeless from Cyclone Gretelle, which hit between January 24 and 26.
The cabinet met on that disaster earlier on Wednesday and a spokesman said it had killed more than 200 people.
An official source said the total number of homeless left without any shelter by the cyclone was estimated at 500,000.
France has sent two Transall transport planes and two Puma helicopters from its island base at Reunion to help rescue work at the request of newly elected Madagascar President Didier Ratsiraka.
In his inaugural address, Ratsiraka who was sworn in on Sunday, said his government would build 35,000 homes each year in the southeast and he had received some aid from donors for the programme.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said last Friday Cyclone Gretelle destroyed up to 90 percent of villages in the southeast when it swept ashore.
It was the worst cyclone to hit Madagascar in living memory. Many of its 14 million people live in chronic poverty.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said floodwaters reached 16 metres (52 feet) deep in places. Winds up to 250 km (155 miles) per hour ripped the roofs off the most substantial buildings such as churches.
Cyclone Gretelle wreaked havoc in a rich southeast farming zone which produces coffee, bananas, oranges and lychees.

The Red Cross said the destruction of crops and food stocks combined with endemic malnutrition in the south of Madagascar and the practice of drinking surface water on the island meant that survivors were extremely vulnerable to hunger and disease.
